title: US-Iran 60-Day MOU Deadline Expires Without a Deal as Nuclear Talks Stall
excerpt: The June 17 memorandum gave both sides two months to reach a final agreement on nuclear issues and the Strait of Hormuz. That window is now closing with no breakthrough in sight.
body:
• The 60-day deadline set by the June 17 US-Iran memorandum of understanding expires around August 17-18 with no final deal reached on nuclear issues or the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Trump has signaled willingness to extend talks past the deadline, telling aides "I don't want to talk about deadlines" — but Iran has declared the MOU "completely dead" after US strikes in July.
  • The OFAC General License permitting Iranian oil trade expires August 21, potentially reimposing full sanctions on Iranian crude exports.
  • Oil markets remain on edge as the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global oil trade before the war, stays largely closed to normal traffic.

The 60-day window for the United States and Iran to negotiate a final deal under their June 17 memorandum of understanding is expiring this week with no agreement in sight, raising the specter of renewed military escalation and fresh disruptions to global energy markets.

The MOU, signed in the Swiss city of Versailles after months of conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, was supposed to create space for a comprehensive settlement. Its 14 points covered a ceasefire, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's nuclear program, a $300 billion reconstruction fund, and the release of frozen Iranian assets. But nearly every pillar of the agreement has fractured.

A Deal That Fell Apart Almost Immediately

The accord's problems began within days of its signing. Iran and the United States managed only two rounds of direct talks — once in Switzerland on June 21 and briefly in Qatar via mediators — before the process stalled. Both sides accused the other of violations. The US struck Iranian military facilities in early July after accusing Iran of hitting commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Foreign Ministry responded by declaring the MOU "completely dead."

https://x.com/clashreport/status/2089256407736414275

"We will not have any negotiation meetings at any level with the American side in the coming days."

— Esmaeil Baghaei, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson

Iran has maintained its right to manage traffic through the Strait of Hormuz jointly with Oman, and has said it plans to impose tolls on vessels — a position Trump has flatly rejected. "It's toll-free, period," Trump said at the G7 summit in June. The standoff over the waterway, which previously carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade, has kept maritime traffic at a fraction of pre-war levels.

What the Deadline Actually Means

Article 3 of the MOU states that the two sides committed to "negotiate and reach a final agreement within a maximum of 60 days, extendable by mutual consent." With the MOU signed June 17-18, the clock runs out around August 17-18.

Trump has already signaled flexibility. According to the Wall Street Journal, he told aides it would be acceptable for talks to extend past the deadline, reportedly saying "I don't want to talk about deadlines. This isn't very important." But experts note that extension requires mutual consent — and Iran may not be willing to provide it.

The expiration has concrete consequences. The Treasury Department's General License X, which authorized transactions related to Iranian crude oil and petroleum products for the first time in 18 years, expires August 21. Without renewal, full sanctions on Iranian oil exports would snap back, cutting off a revenue stream that Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian had called "a great victory for the Iranian people."

Nuclear Talks at an Impasse

The most ambitious element of the MOU — resolving the nuclear issue within 60 days — was always considered unrealistic by most analysts. The key sticking points remain unresolved: the US wants Iran's enrichment capped at 5 percent, while Iran insists on maintaining 20 percent capacity. Iran has also refused to allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to visit bombed nuclear sites where its highly enriched uranium is believed to be buried.

A Polymarket prediction contract on whether Iran would agree to a one-year enrichment moratorium by year-end currently trades at very low odds, reflecting broad skepticism about a breakthrough.

What Comes Next

The path forward is uncertain. Trump has discussed further strikes with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine but has held off, telling aides that "a full-scale attack could undermine the possibility of dismantling Iran's nuclear program," according to the Wall Street Journal.

For the Indian diaspora and markets watchers, the implications are direct. Oil prices, which spiked above $100 a barrel when the Strait of Hormuz closed, remain elevated. Any breakdown in talks could send them higher still, with cascading effects on inflation, consumer prices, and the November midterm elections that Trump is watching closely.

France's President Macron has offered to cooperate with Oman on de-mining the strait. Qatar and Pakistan continue to serve as mediators. But with both Washington and Tehran dug into their positions and the formal negotiating window closing, the conflict that has already reshaped global energy markets shows no sign of resolution.
